accuracy.evidence: Checked every number in the lesson and lab: pencil 9 cm, end at the ruler edge 0.8 cm before 0 gives a tip reading of 8.2 cm (less than the length); 4 marks between 200 and 300 ml make 5 intervals of 100 ÷ 5 = 20 ml, so 260 ml is the 3rd mark; thermometer marks 10 ÷ 5 = 2 °C; 150 g bowl + 180 g apple = 330 g; 400 − 150 = 250 g of flour. Parallax direction (from above reads too high, from below too low) matches Carolina's graduated-cylinder guide (75 mL true, 76 mL from above) and the lab computes it geometrically from a sight line to the centre of the surface. Curriculum wording checked against NC 2013 Years 3-4 working scientifically ('take accurate measurements using standard units, using a range of equipment, including thermometers and data loggers'). Parameterised items checked at range corners: p2 b − a (6..13), p3 100h + 20k (120..480), p4 t − b (140..280), m2 10h + 2k (12..38), m5 j.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented primary measurement errors (NCETM measures guidance; Nunes, Light & Mason 1993 on children reading a ruler from its end; parallax in Carolina/CUNY lab manuals): measuring from the ruler's end (step 1 prediction, challenge tags tip and add); counting each mark as 1 or dividing by marks instead of intervals (step 2 prediction 1 ml / 25 ml, tags ones and quarter, m7); reading from above (step 3 prediction, tags low and twice, m1); ignoring the container's mass (step 4 prediction 180 g / 30 g, tags whole and plus, p4); reading a thermometer before it settles or averaging warm-up readings (step 5 prediction, tags first and avg, m4); and picking the wrong instrument or unit (tags jug and scales, m3).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagscale is about measuring technique, not what a quantity is: a ruler whose 0 sits in from the edge, a jug scale whose interval must be worked out, a side-view sight line whose crossing with the scale is the reading you see, kitchen scales with a working tare button, and a data-logger graph that flattens as a thermometer settles. flagtherm teaches what a thermometer shows (ages 5-7), flagunits picks units, flagweigh/flagcups measure with non-standard units; none has a zero offset, parallax, tare or settling. 6-shingle similarity is at most 4.5% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each habit is discovered before it is stated: the pencil tip reads 8.2 cm until its end reaches 0 and then 9 cm; narration counts water in marks (3 marks above 200), so the learner must work out 20 ml a mark to hit 260; the 'You read' label falls from about 330 ml (iPhone width) to 300 ml as the eye is lowered to the water; the display shows 330 g (bowl and apple) until Zero is pressed with only the bowl on, then 180 g; early 'Read now' presses are flagged 'still rising: too low' and only three matching readings after the graph flattens complete the task.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'its true length' (tip shows 8.2 cm, not 9); '1 ml' and '25 ml' per mark (marks step 20 ml); 'the right amount' when looking from above (the label reads about 330 ml for 300); '180 g' with the bowl on (display shows 330 g); 'right' for an instant thermometer reading (graph starts at 20 °C and climbs to 40 °C).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Twelve distinct wrong-answer messages, each naming the slip: tip (read where it ends but it started at 2), add (do not add the marks), ones (a mark is not 1 ml), quarter (4 marks make 5 gaps, not 4), low (from above is too high, not too low), twice (repeating from the same wrong place repeats the error), whole (that includes the bowl), plus (do not add the bowl again), first (read while still rising), avg (do not average warm-up readings), jug and scales (wrong tool for temperature).

readability.evidence: validate_lessons passes (family audience): kid text FK 2.1 (limit 5.0), adult FK 5.4 (limit 10.0). Units are named in words with their symbols the first time (centimetres (cm), millilitres (ml), grams (g), degrees Celsius (°C)); every rule comes with a worked number (9 − 2 = 7 cm, 100 ÷ 5 = 20 ml). Lab step texts are two or three short sentences; buttons say exactly what they do (Pour in one mark, Eye down, Press ZERO, Wait 10 seconds, Read now).

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passes (no banned phrases; explanation overlap with every lesson under 12%). Kid paragraphs: tools and units; start at zero with a worked example; mark value and eye level; tare, settling and repeats with data logger defined. Adult paragraphs: curriculum statement and key words; named common mistakes; what accuracy and repeats can and cannot fix; what each lab step does.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots on iPhone 13 (390 px, dark), a 360 px Android viewport (light) and desktop (dark) before and after Show me on all six steps. First pass had jug labels overlapping the scale numbers at 360 px and guide lines that vanished on the yellow ruler in dark mode; fixed by moving the jug to the left edge with shorter labels and drawing guides in dark ink on the ruler. Ruler shows half-centimetre ticks and every other number below 22 px per cm; the eye is a 44 x 26 px drag target; scale and buttons stay unclipped; control buttons wrap two to a row.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button: Slide left/right, Pour in/out one mark, Eye up/down, Put bowl on/Put apple in/Press ZERO, Wait 10 seconds/Read now; challenge answers are buttons labelled 'Answer: …'. speak() updates the canvas aria-label and the visible narration after every action (e.g. 'The water is 3 marks above 200', 'From above you read 340 ml. Too high'). walk.cjs: desktop and iPhone 13 complete all 5 tasks with Show me, the challenge shows, axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes, no console errors. Canvas text sits on light cards with dark ink in both themes.
